stem:
A 30-year-old at 34 weeks, whose booking blood pressure was 112/70 mmHg, has readings of 152/98 and 150/96 mmHg four hours apart. She has new swelling of her hands and face and has gained 2 kg this week. She has no headache, visual symptoms or epigastric pain. Urine dipstick shows 1+ protein, but the protein:creatinine ratio is 16 mg/mmol (significant ≥30). Creatinine is 104 µmol/L (58 at booking), platelets 212 × 10^9/L, ALT 24 U/L, and uric acid is raised.

Which diagnosis best accounts for these findings?

options.label: A
options.text: Gestational hypertension, as the protein:creatinine ratio is below 30
options.explanation: New hypertension after 20 weeks with any organ involvement is pre-eclampsia; proteinuria is not required, and her creatinine is raised.

options.label: B
options.text: Chronic kidney disease unmasked by the demands of pregnancy
options.explanation: Her booking creatinine was normal, so the rise is new in pregnancy rather than pre-existing kidney disease.

options.label: C
options.text: Pre-eclampsia, with renal involvement shown by the creatinine
options.explanation: A creatinine above 90 µmol/L with new hypertension after 20 weeks counts as renal involvement, so this is pre-eclampsia despite a normal protein:creatinine ratio. Oedema, weight gain, uric acid and a 1+ dipstick are not criteria.

options.label: D
options.text: HELLP syndrome evolving from gestational hypertension
options.explanation: HELLP needs haemolysis, raised liver enzymes and low platelets; her platelets and ALT are normal.

options.label: E
options.text: Chronic hypertension first detected in the third trimester
options.explanation: Her booking blood pressure was normal and the hypertension began after 20 weeks, so it is not chronic.

context: Pre-eclampsia is new hypertension after 20 weeks with any organ involvement; a creatinine above 90 µmol/L is renal involvement even when the protein:creatinine ratio is normal.
